questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That is was a different culture than what I'm used to, and that they had at least some courses available that I found relevant. I also found it important that it wasn't too expensive a country to live in.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It has for sure been the best thing i every did

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I studiet at science where they were pretty well organized, so before the first introduction day, I got emails informing me about where to meet up and what to do. And if I had any questions i just texted them and they would respond pretty quickly. And at the first introduction day we got a lot of information that made you pretty well informed.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Emails, the introduction meeting, and a tour around campus, and a trip to the bar in the evening. We were also added to bigger WhatsApp groups where you could ask each other for information.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was not so hard I would say. I found an organization called "student republic". They have different residents located around Prague. I lived in Tesla residence, located in Prague 1, so very centered and good location, and also close to science. I got a single room which was nice but also more expensive. I can say a lot of stuff about the state of the apartments, like they weren't so clean and the walls are super thin and stuff, but the overall experience was just fine and worked pretty well for me. But if you choose this place, when it comes to the payment of the rent, ask to get the Czech IBAN, it makes it way more easy. 
I know others who lived in buildings just for Erasmus students, also in the city centre near the place i stayed. I can also recommend that.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It's nice to live in the city and close to everything, but a lot of my friends chose to stay at the dorms, which is a bit far away, although easy to reach with public transport. But it could also have been fun to stay with them at the dorms even tho the quality of the dorms is really low, but so is the rent.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: There is a catalogue with a long list of courses available, but you have to be carefull as both summer and winter courses are listed. many of the courses have a very low amount of credits, like 2-5, which means you will be having a lot of courses if you don't pick some of the courses with more credits.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: there was the Erasmus office at the faculty, but she wasn't always the easiest to communicate with, but I didn't have to, so it worked out fine for me

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: very, I had no problems, but I did hear from some of my friends that they might only let you attend one field course, so just keep that in mind when you choose your courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try not to change courses too much maybe, and get a lot of courses pre-approved from home. It made it easier to change if you wanted to.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Not so many relevant courses for a Landscape architect, but it worked out.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Well I just had MA courses, I would say that there was a lot available in english.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The academic level of the courses is generally lower than at UCPH I would say, and the exams were pretty chill. But that was really nice since you most likely want to spend time on friends and fun. But ofc it depends on which courses you take and what you study. It was higher levels for the Biologists for an example. 
I spent way less time on the campus in Prague than i do in Copenhagen. most classes are lecture-based that only last 1-2 hours and you only have it once a week.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
General Ecology
Field Course in Botany 
Practical internship in Botany - 10 days 
Forest Geography 
Urban health 
Urban social geography: contemporary issues 
Land use, landscape and society

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Field Course in Botany : it was easy and fun to experience. a lot of czechs and czech food. you learn a lot, but it is often placed in the end of may or the beginning of june, which crashes a bit with exams or end of erasmus, cause you will be gone for 6 days. 

Practical internship in Botany - 10 days : nice way to get credits, its different form lectures which is nice. but get it done in the beginning of the semester, so you have more free time in the end. 

Urban health and Urban social geography : actually really relevant for a landscape architect, and nice courses 

General Ecology : this was tough but you learned a lot. 

Forest Geography : a lot of it was relevant and you will already have heard of many of the terms, but some of it not so much, since there was also remote sensing and stuff.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
I had to go to the doctor once, but my insurance covered it, but not the medicine. 
You want to explore the country and probably travel to other places while on exchange, and that will cost you. 
Going out a lot always gets a bit expensive at some point even tho beer is very cheap in Czech. 
You had to pay for the field course, and for the introduction trip.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
It's cheaper to eat out than it is to buy groceries.
Its crazy cheap to use public transportation in Czech when you are a student, compared to Denmark. I think i payed 130Dkk for unlimited use of every form of public transport in Prague for three months.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Erasmus club (which is only at science) did an introduction trip that you REALLY should attend. They also organized other events which was great. 
You could register for sports courses which gave you 1 credit, but i think they speak czech, but you can still attend.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Go on the introduction trip!!! you really create good relations there. 
Take trips outside of Prague and explore the country.
Go on the trips arranged by "Erasmus in Prague" they are super fun and you meet nice people 
Go to Berlin for the first of may

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go see other Czech cities or go on the trips arranged by Erasmus in Prague! its super fun to explore a bit.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy I would say, I was there a small week before so I was pretty well adapted when it all started. But you have to get used to some rudeness from the locals.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It doesn't really happen unless you take a Czech course I would say. It was only at my internship and ad the field course that I spoke to other czech students. And also at the Urbn health class they mixed the groups so there was at least one czech person in each group.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not many, other than czech people who didn't speak english or people in service who were kind of rude.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The city is so beautiful, and you feel very safe in it, also in the night life I would say. I loved the Trams and the public transport was super easy. You can dress however, the people are not controversial or anything.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Go on the organized trips, you really get great experiences on them. 
Go on trips to other countries and make memories 
Go have fun in the city and try out dirfferent city parts, everything is really cheap compared to Copenhagen so take advantage of it!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Fio Banka - a band that does not charge you extra fees when you withdraw money. 
Many of the exams are not hard to pass, but some are sand it is possible to fail. But the teachers are usually really nice and if you tal to them, they might cut you some slag.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: the people. I got some amazing friends from all over the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: making time for everything you wanted to do, while keeping up with school and budget.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
